client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my thesis deadline is creeping up and I honestly don't know how I'm going to get everything done in time. On top of that, I'm still working my part-time job and trying to keep up with friends, and it all just feels like too much at once. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day the deadlines are still going to be there no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — juggling your thesis, work, and friendships all at once — and that sense of "it's all too much" makes complete sense given everything on your plate. You're right that talking won't erase the deadlines, but what it *can* do is help us untangle some of the thoughts that might be making the weight feel even heavier than it needs to be. I'm curious — when you imagine not getting everything done in time, what's the story your mind tells you about what that would mean?

client: Honestly, when I imagine not finishing my thesis on time, my mind goes straight to this place of "you're a failure and everyone will finally see it." Like, my advisor, my parents, even my friends — I picture them all kind of stepping back and realizing they were wrong to believe in me. It's not just about the deadline, it feels like the whole thing would prove something I've been scared is true about me for a long time.
therapist: That takes real courage to name — this fear that missing a deadline would somehow expose a deeper truth about you that you've been quietly carrying for a long time. What I want to gently point out is that your mind has taken one possible outcome and turned it into *proof* of something about your whole worth as a person, which is a really painful place to be. I'd love to explore that belief a little — what actual evidence do you have, from your life so far, that the people around you are just waiting to find a reason to withdraw their belief in you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but honestly, when I try to think of evidence, my mind just goes straight to all the times people *have* pulled back when I've struggled. Like my old manager who stopped including me in meetings after I asked for an extension once, or friends who seem to drift away whenever I'm not at my best. I know you might say those are just coincidences or there were other reasons, but it's hard not to see a pattern there.
therapist: It makes sense that those experiences feel like evidence — they're real and they hurt, and it's completely natural for our minds to connect them into a pattern, especially when we're already worried about being "found out." What I'd gently invite you to consider is whether there might be another explanation for those moments — your manager and those friends — that has nothing to do with your worth, even if it doesn't feel as convincing right now. Can you think of anyone in your life who has *stayed* or even leaned in closer during a time when you were struggling?

client: I mean... my sister, maybe. She kind of showed up more when I was going through that really bad patch last year, kept texting me even when I wasn't responding much. But honestly, part of me wonders if that's just because she's family and she has to, you know? Like it doesn't really count the same way.
therapist: It's really meaningful that your sister showed up for you like that — and I notice how quickly your mind moved to discount it, as if there's a rule that love or loyalty "doesn't count" unless it comes without any obligation. That discounting is worth paying attention to, because it means your mind might be filtering out evidence that challenges the belief that people leave when you struggle. What do you think it would mean for that core fear if you allowed her showing up to count as real?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept it, but there's this other part that keeps whispering "she only came because she felt like she had to." If I let her showing up actually count, then I'd have to admit that maybe I've been wrong about people leaving, and honestly that's almost scarier than just staying with the belief I already have. It's like the loneliness is familiar, and letting it crack open feels more dangerous than just keeping it intact.
therapist: What you just said is incredibly insightful — recognizing that the familiar pain of loneliness can feel *safer* than the vulnerability of letting someone's love in is a really profound thing to notice about yourself. That protective belief has probably kept you from getting hurt in certain ways, but it sounds like it's also been quietly keeping you from feeling truly seen and supported, even when that support is right there. What do you think that younger part of you was trying to protect you from when it first learned that keeping people at a distance was the safer choice?

client: I think that younger part of me was trying to protect me from the feeling of needing someone and then having them just... not show up. Like, if I never really let people in, I couldn't be disappointed or abandoned. But saying that out loud feels kind of raw, because it also means I've been doing that to people who actually do care about me now, and that makes me feel guilty on top of everything else.
therapist: What you just shared is really tender and brave — that younger version of you made a completely understandable choice to stay safe, and it worked in the way it needed to at the time. The guilt you're feeling now actually speaks to something important: it means you *do* want real connection, and you're aware enough to see where the wall has been. Rather than adding guilt to everything else you're carrying, I wonder if you could hold this as a moment of clarity rather than a verdict — what might it look like to let one person, maybe your sister, in just a little more than you have been?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that framing — that it's clarity, not a verdict. But when I think about letting my sister in more, there's this immediate tightening in my chest, like... what if I do that and she still doesn't really get me, or she says something that makes me feel worse? I've tried before and it didn't go the way I hoped, so it's hard to trust that this time would be different.
therapist: That tightening in your chest is worth honoring — it's your nervous system remembering a real hurt, and it makes complete sense that past disappointments would make your body want to protect you from trying again. What I'd gently offer is that "letting her in" doesn't have to mean one big vulnerable conversation where everything is on the line — it could be something much smaller, like responding to one of her texts a little more honestly than you normally would. What would feel like the tiniest, most manageable step toward connection that still feels safe enough to actually try?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that a small step could actually work. But the thing is, even texting her back more honestly feels risky, because what if she takes that as an opening and then I get pulled into something I'm not ready for? I guess I'm scared that any crack in the door means she'll push it wide open, and I won't know how to handle that.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — like opening up even a little means losing control of how much comes in, and after working so hard to manage that door, the idea of it swinging open feels overwhelming. What's worth noticing here is that *you* get to decide how wide the door opens — one honest text doesn't hand her the handle, and you can set the pace of this. What would it feel like to know that you're allowed to be in control of how much you share, even as you let a little more in?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true — that I can control the pace. But honestly, in my experience, once you give someone a little, they start expecting more, and then you're either pulling back and hurting them or you're in deeper than you meant to be. It's like the "control" thing sounds good in theory but I'm not sure it actually works that way with real people.
therapist: Your experience has genuinely taught you that boundaries don't always hold the way you hope, and that's a real and valid thing to have learned — not just a distortion. What I'm curious about though is whether the pattern you're describing might also be connected to how hard it is for you to *say* "that's enough for now" out loud to someone, rather than just quietly withdrawing. What do you think gets in the way of you being able to tell someone directly, even your sister, "I want to connect but I need to go slowly"?

client: Honestly, even just imagining saying that to my sister out loud makes my stomach tighten up. I think part of me is afraid that if I tell her I need to go slowly, she'll take it as rejection and pull away completely, and then I'll have made things worse by trying to protect myself. It's like I'm stuck between two bad options — get overwhelmed by too much closeness too fast, or lose the connection entirely by being honest about what I need.
therapist: That feeling of being trapped between two painful options is really exhausting, and it makes sense that your body is reacting to even the thought of it. But I want to gently reflect something back to you — the belief that honesty about your needs will push people away is itself worth examining, because right now it's the thing standing between you and any possibility of real connection. What do you actually know about your sister that might tell you how she'd *really* respond if you told her you wanted to be close but needed to take it slowly?
